meta.title: SPACE-KBP: A Dataset for End-to-End Knowledge Base Population in the Space Mission Domain
meta.authorsHtml: José Manuel Gómez-Pérez<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Cristian Berrío<sup>2</sup>, Andrés García-Silva<sup>3</sup>

abstract: We present SPACE-KBP, to the best of our knowledge the first dataset for end-to-end knowledge base population (KBP) in the space mission domain. The dataset is constructed from textual mission descriptions and structured domain resources, and is aligned with the ESA space mission ontology. It provides paired inputs and outputs for generating ontology-compliant RDF triples, enabling the training and evaluation of large language models (LLMs) for end-to-end KBP. As a case study, we use SPACE-KBP to populate a space mission knowledge graph by fine-tuning LLMs of varying sizes. Our experiments show that compact, domain-specialized models achieve competitive, and in some cases superior, performance compared with larger models. Furthermore, after fine-tuning on SPACE-KBP, the models no longer require explicit ontology descriptions in the prompt, indicating that the required ontology knowledge is effectively captured during fine-tuning. These findings show that compact models and shorter prompts improve deployment efficiency while reducing computational cost for domain-specific KBP.

blocks.html: Knowledge graphs represent domain and world knowledge by organizing entities and their relationships as a graph [1, 2]. While widely used in applications such as search engines, recommenders [3], and chatbots [4], their utility depends on accurate and comprehensive population [5, 6], which is often a labor-intensive task. Knowledge base population (KBP) [7] aims at automating this task, generating structured knowledge from text corpora. However, traditional KBP pipelines are error-prone [8], comprising multiple steps such as entity linking [9], slot-filling [10], and relation extraction [11]. In contrast, end-to-end approaches leverage sequence-to-sequence models [12] where a decoder [8, 13] generates triples directly from input sentences or paragraphs, while often overlooking knowledge that could be otherwise drawn from entire texts.

State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) can extract ontology instances from long texts end-to-end, generating RDF [14] serializations annotated with widely used ontologies such as Dublin Core<sup>1</sup> or FOAF<sup>2</sup>, which are well represented in their pre-training data. However, in specialized domains, which are typically less represented, this requires domain ontologies to be explicitly included in the prompt, increasing the token count and therefore API costs. A further limitation is the scarcity of exhaustively annotated datasets for end-to-end KBP, as fully labeling all extractable triples can be prohibitively costly [15]. Thus, KBP datasets such as the NIST TAC KBP corpus [7, 16], KnowledgeNet [17], and WIKI [8], as well as relation extraction datasets like T-REx [18], FewRel [19], and TACRED [20], tend to rely on encyclopedic knowledge bases such as Wikidata, which are too general for specialized domains requiring domain-specific ontologies.

Rather than large general LLMs behind paywalls, or hosted in costly on-premise infrastructures, we advocate for smaller LLMs that can be adapted as domain-specific KBP specialists in specialized domains via supervised finetuning. This offers practical advantages such as lower computational requirements, faster inference, and reduced overall costs. Therefore, we propose using larger models only once to distill training data, extracting ontologycompliant instances from text and formalizing them in an RDF serialization such as Turtle<sup>3</sup>, as illustrated in Figure 1.

We introduce SPACE-KBP, a dataset for training and evaluating end-to-end KBP systems in the space mission domain. As a case study, we examine the European Space Agency’s (ESA) space mission ontology [21], which supports data integration and information discovery in the space mission domain. To validate SPACE-KBP, we finetune the Pythia language models [22], ranging from 14 million to 12 billion parameters, and analyze model scale versus KBP performance. Our results confirm that compact, domain-specialized LLMs in the order of 1-2.8 billion parameters can be effectively adapted for KBP, remaining competitive and even outperforming larger variants. Our data, models, prompts, and code are publicly available. <sup>45</sup>

The space mission ontology [21] models space missions, instruments, orbit, and stakeholders, as well as the countries involved in each mission (see Table 1). Originally, the ontology was not available in RDF. Therefore, we implement it using Protegé6 in Turtle format.

blocks.html: ESA’s EOPortal7 contains descriptions of more than 1,200 space missions, including mission overview, space segment, instruments, and ground segment, as well as information about launch and status. We use EOPortal as textual source to extract ontology-aligned triples.

CEOS8, the database of the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites. We download structured information for 725 space missions and 1,055 instruments. Of these, 172 missions are also in EOPortal, which we use to evaluate both the generated train set and KBP model outputs.

To fine-tune an LLM to populate a space mission knowledge graph, we need a dataset with tuples containing the instructions prompting the model to extract individuals from the ontology, the input text describing the mission, and the expected output, with the extracted individuals in Turtle format. The instructions are hand-crafted and include a textual description of the space mission ontology.

The mission descriptions in EOPortal can be considerably long. Therefore, including them directly in the sequences used to train the LLM could exceed its context window. Given that the Pythia models used in our study have a maximum sequence length of 2,048 tokens, we instruct a pre-trained model, Llama3-8B<sup>9</sup>, to generate threeto-four-paragraph summaries of each mission, focusing on key information captured by the ontology, such as launch date, objectives, orbit, instruments, and stakeholders.

Since Llama3-8B is Turtle-aware, we instruct it to extract the ontology individuals from the mission summary in Turtle, following a dialogue structure. First, the model is asked to acknowledge whether it understands the mission ontology that follows in plain text. Then, it responds, providing a brief summary of the ontology. Then, the model is instructed to extract instances of the ontology from a mission description summary. An example of the task is provided to the model. The response consists of the ontology instances extracted from the input text.

A total 1,060 mission descriptions from EOPortal were processed. We manually inspect the result and observe that Llama3-8B does not generate syntactically valid Turtle representations for the majority of missions. Moreover, in some cases the triples do not respect the range and domain constraints of the properties. Therefore, we adopt an iterative approach that combines LLM-generated outputs with human corrections. First, we define and manually apply heuristics at the lexico-syntactical and semantic level to fix non-valid Turtle, making it compliant with the ontology schema. In the following iteration only the missions that still have non-valid Turtle are processed.

Our heuristics are as follows. Lexico-syntactic corrections include replacing all namespaces in the generated Turtle with the correct ones, adding default time to dates without time, removing triplets with unknown or empty dates, and removing preceding question marks from entity names. Semantic corrections include deleting all triples that do not comply with the domain or range constraints expressed in the ontology and automatically relating isolated instruments and orbits to the mission entity. From the 1,060 mission descriptions initially processed from EOPortal, we obtain syntactically valid Turtle respecting domain and range constraints for 1,025 across nine generation rounds. As shown in Table 2, the systematic replacement of namespaces (NS) is the heuristic with the greatest impact.

Pythia [22] includes 10 LLMs of variable size ranging from 14 million to 12 billion parameters. All the models were trained following the same approach on The Pile corpus, which covers domains such as books, GitHub repositories, and web pages among others. We select models pre-trained on the deduplicated version of The Pile whenever available. The Pythia suite allows comparing the results of the finetuning process on the KBP task across different model sizes.

blocks.html: To train the Pythia models for the KBP task we perform supervised fine-tuning on the SPACE-KBP set. The learning objective is the language modeling task, i.e., next token prediction, although in this case the text consists of pairs of instructions and responses: the instruction includes the ontology and the mission description; the response is the extracted individuals in Turtle. From the dataset introduced in the previous section, we build a test set with the 174 missions with corresponding structured data in CEOS. The remaining 851 missions are used for training.

We fine-tune the Pythia models with and without adding the ontology in the instruction. All models are trained for 7 steps with effective batch size 8, learning rate 2e-5, AdamW optimizer, and early stopping after two consecutive steps. Each model was trained for a maximum of 700 steps, hence each model sees approximately 7 times the training set (106 steps per epoch) at most. To reduce the number of training parameters for 2.8B and larger models, we apply LoRA [23], with rank 16 and scaling factor α 32, targeting the key-value matrices of the attention blocks. All training and inference is done on a single A100 NVIDIA GPU with 40GB VRAM.

Figure 2 shows the percentage of syntactically valid Turtle generated by the fine-tuned models. As shown in the figure, the smallest 14M and 70M models are unable to produce correct Turtle, whereas models with 160M parameters and larger consistently generate syntactically valid outputs. Compared to LLaMA-3-8B in zero-shot without task-specific fine-tuning, fine-tuned models with 410M parameters or more produce a higher percentage of valid Turtle code. From 1B parameters onward, the fine-tuned models generate 90% or more of syntactically correct Turtle code, showing evidence that the fine-tuned models have effectively learned the task. Adding the ontology to the prompt slightly hurts performance for 2.8B models and larger, while benefiting models of 1B and 1.4B parameters.

To semantically evaluate the generation of the fine-tuned models against the CEOS database, we run SPARQL queries on the Turtle generated by the models, retrieving the textual property values of the ontology individuals. Each value is then compared with the ground truth text of the corresponding CEOS attribute. We use two complementary metrics: a lexical metric such as ROUGE-L and a semantic text similarity score provided by an LLM. To address any circularity concerns, we use Qwen3-8B<sup>10</sup> instead of Llama3- 8B, which was used in the generation of SPACE-KBP.

blocks.html: Tables 3 and 4 report ROUGE-L and LLM similarity in average and per ontology property, considering those that are represented in the test set. The best models, 2.8B and 12B in that order, are fine-tuned without including the ontology in the prompt. Llama3-8B zero-shot is included in the table as a reference since we use it to distill SPACE-KBP. Note that Llama3-8B only generates valid turtle for 49% of the missions, while our 1B and larger models fine-tuned on SPACE- KBP produce more than 90% valid Turtle. For properties such as Objectives or Instrument Application, ROUGE-L produces heterogeneous and low scores compared to those of the LLM-based similarity metric. This is because the generation of the fine-tuned model is much more concise than the ground truth from the CEOS database. In those cases, LLM-based similarity yields higher scores because the judge focuses on the meaning of the texts and does not rely as much as ROUGE-L on their lexical representation.

Excluding the ontology from the prompt consistently yields better results for 1B parameter models onward. This finding is of practical relevance, as shorter prompts are processed more efficiently, reducing inference time and GPU memory usage and lowering operational costs. 160M parameter models or smaller fail to learn the extraction of property values. The best overall performance is achieved by the 2.8B model, followed by the 12B and 6.9B models; however, the 1B model remains competitive, constituting a viable option in low-compute scenarios. The fact that the 2.8B model outperforms the 6.9B and 12B variants, shows that increasing model size beyond a certain point does not necessarily lead to better performance in this case.

We introduced SPACE-KBP, to the best of our knowledge the first dataset for end-to-end knowledge base population (KBP) in the space mission domain. The dataset pairs mission description summaries with ontology-compliant RDF representations aligned with the ESA space mission ontology, enabling the supervised training and evaluation of large language models for knowledge graph population.

Our results demonstrate that the proposed dataset construction methodology provides sufficient structural and semantic supervision for end-to-end RDF generation. Models fine-tuned on SPACE-KBP consistently produce ontologycompliant outputs, with models of 1B parameters and larger generating syntactically valid Turtle in more than 90% of cases. These results show that the automatically constructed training data effectively supports ontology-aligned knowledge extraction.

Among the evaluated models, those in the 1B–2.8B parameter range achieve the best trade-off between syntactic validity and semantic accuracy. Furthermore, removing the ontology description from the prompt improves performance for models larger than 1B parameters, indicating that the required ontology knowledge is effectively captured during fine-tuning. This has practical implications for operational deployments, where shorter prompts reduce both latency and computational cost.

Our experiments also show that KBP performance does not increase monotonically with model size. The 2.8B model outperforms both the 6.9B and 12B variants, while models with 160M parameters or fewer fail to reliably learn structured RDF generation. These findings indicate that moderately sized, domain-specialized models provide the most effective solution for this task.

SPACE-KBP provides a benchmark for developing and evaluating end-to-end KBP systems in the space mission domain, while establishing a reproducible methodology for constructing ontology-aligned training data from complementary textual and structured resources. Future work will investigate the scalability of the dataset construction methodology to larger and more expressive ontologies, evaluate additional model families, assess transferability to other application domains, and extend the framework to multimodal knowledge base population.
